newsitem.title: USA: Soybean prices fall, rain boosts crop outlook.
newsitem.headline: Soybean prices fall, rain boosts crop outlook.

text.p: Soybean prices fell sharply Monday as much needed rains soaked crops in the Midwest, improving the prospects for this year's harvest.
"The (rainy) weather finally came in Sunday afternoon and Sunday night after a long weekend of waiting for it," said Jerry Gidel, analyst with Dean Witter in Chicago.

"There are prospects for some more rains continuing in certain spots through Wednesday," he added. "The corn market seems to feel some damage may have already been done but beans could see some improvement back above trend-line yields."

Crops in parts of Illinois and Indiana, both leading corn and soybean producing states, have been starved of moisture in recent weeks. In Indianapolis rainfall for the 30 days up to Sunday was only 10 percent of normal, according to data issued by Weather Services Corp.
At the Chicago Board of Trade soybeans for November delivery closed down 27-1/2 cents a bushel at $6.10, just above an earlier two-week low of $6.09.
News of crop boosting rains also depressed corn prices although losses were much more modest.
"It (the market) did exactly what it should have done. The rain was bearish for beans and probably a little too late for corn," said Charlie Sernatinger, analyst for E.D. and F. Man International
"Corn is already pollinated and we may be able to get a little better test weight but it won't help the yields much," he noted.
CBOT corn for December delivery closed 3-3/4 cents lower at $2.53-1/4 a bushel.

Gold prices were higher, boosted by ongoing nervousness about the direction of U.S. stocks and bonds, as the market continued to slowly recover after last month's slide to the lowest levels for around 12 years.

"Gold looks like it's still trying to find a bottom, helped by the rise in U.S. interest rates and nervousness about the stock market, but the long downtrend may not be over yet and there's not much fundamental reason to be bullish on gold," Pioneer Futures analyst Scott Meyers said.
At the New York Commodity Exchange (COMEX) gold for December delivery closed up $2.10 an ounce at $332.50, its highest closing level since late July.

"Friday's breakdown in financial markets was quite severe and may not be over yet, but the trade wants to sell gold around $333 (on the COMEX December contract)," North American Equity Services COMEX floor trader, John Geraghty, said.

Platinum lost a little ground on news South Africa's Impala Platinum Holdings (Implats), one of the world's largest suppliers of platinum group metals, had settled a seven day old strike at its refineries.
Implats produced about 499,000 ounces of refined platinum in the six months ended December 1996 and normal output is about one million ounces a year.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) platinum for October delivery finished down $1.70 at $442.00 an ounce.
NYMEX oil prices took a breather Monday following sharp declines last week with crude and heating oil inching higher in what many traders called listless trade.
"It was kind of consolidation day for the crude and heating oil," said Tom Bentz, energy analyst at High Yield Analytics in New York.
Traders said they were digesting news of resumption to Iraqi oil sales under the humanitarian exception to broad UN sanctions following Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
While the news sparked last week's selloff, its longer terms effects are not yet clear.
Crude oil for September delivery rose 15 cents to settle at $19.69 a barrel.
In the gasoline pit prices were helped lower by news a key East Coast refiner was returning a big crude processing unit to service a bit sooner than expected following maintenance.
Unleaded gasoline futures for September delivery settled 0.52 cent lower at 61.47 a gallon.
Heating oil futures for September delivery settled 0.07 cent higher at 54.36 cents a gallon.
